academic_passage.title: Island Biogeography
academic_passage.text: Ecologists have long observed that islands differ in the number of species they contain. One influential explanation is the theory of island biogeography, which proposes that species richness reflects a balance between immigration and extinction. Islands located closer to a mainland source are more likely to receive new species because organisms can reach them more easily. Larger islands, meanwhile, generally support larger populations and a wider range of habitats, reducing the chance that species will disappear locally.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why mainland habitats contain no extinctions
How island size and isolation can influence species richness
Why all islands have similar species

questions.q: Why are islands closer to a mainland likely to receive more species?
options: Organisms can reach them more easily.

academic_passage.title: The Spread of Printing
academic_passage.text: The rapid spread of printing in fifteenth-century Europe did more than increase the number of books in circulation. It changed how scholars compared sources, how merchants distributed practical manuals, and how religious debates reached audiences beyond local communities. Printed works were not automatically accurate, but identical copies made it easier for readers in different cities to discuss the same passage. Over time, this shared textual base encouraged more systematic criticism and helped create networks of readers who had never met.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why printed books were always inexpensive
How printing affected communication and scholarship

questions.q: According to the passage, what did identical copies make easier?
options: Discussing the same passage in different cities
Teaching people to write by hand

They may have varied more from copy to copy.

questions.q: Why does the author mention merchants?
options: To show that printing influenced everyday professional activity
To argue that merchants invented printing
To contrast books with religious objects

questions.q: Which outcome developed over time?
options: A shared base for criticism among readers

academic_passage.title: Coral Reef Symbiosis
academic_passage.text: Coral reefs depend on a delicate relationship between coral animals and microscopic algae that live inside their tissues. The algae use sunlight to produce sugars, some of which are transferred to the coral. In return, the algae receive shelter and access to compounds they need for photosynthesis. When ocean temperatures remain unusually high, this relationship can break down, and corals may expel the algae. The resulting bleaching does not always kill the coral immediately, but it leaves the organism with far less energy.

options: A predator-prey relationship between fish and coral
A mutually beneficial relationship between coral and algae
A competition between algae and sunlight
A process by which coral eats sand

questions.q: Why does the author describe what each organism receives?
options: To explain why the relationship benefits both partners
To show that algae harm coral tissues
To argue that photosynthesis is impossible underwater

academic_passage.title: Urban Archaeology
academic_passage.text: Urban archaeology often requires researchers to work within active cities, where construction schedules, underground utilities, and public safety rules limit excavation. These constraints can make the work difficult, yet they also provide unusual opportunities. Layers beneath streets may preserve evidence of markets, workshops, and household routines that written records ignored. By combining small excavations with maps, tax documents, and environmental samples, archaeologists can reconstruct how ordinary residents used urban space over long periods.

options: How archaeologists study ordinary life in cities
Why cities prevent all historical research
Why markets disappeared from urban areas

options: They combine several kinds of evidence.

academic_passage.title: The Development of Maps
academic_passage.text: Maps are often treated as neutral representations of space, but every map reflects choices about purpose and audience. A navigation map may emphasize roads and landmarks while ignoring soil type or property ownership. A geological map, by contrast, may show rock formations in great detail while simplifying streets. Because maps select and organize information, historians use them not only to locate places but also to understand how societies valued territory, resources, and movement at particular moments in time.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How maps reflect choices and social priorities

questions.q: According to the passage, what might a navigation map emphasize?

academic_passage.title: Insect Pollination Networks
academic_passage.text: Pollination is often described as a simple exchange between one plant and one insect, yet most ecosystems contain complex networks of interactions. A single bee species may visit many kinds of flowers, and a single plant species may depend on several pollinators. This overlap can make communities more resilient when one species declines, but it can also allow disturbances to spread through the network. Researchers study these patterns to predict which plants may be most vulnerable to changes in land use, climate, or pesticide exposure.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The anatomy of a single bee species

questions.q: What can make pollination communities resilient?

Plants may stop producing flowers immediately.

options: To predict which plants face risks

academic_passage.title: Apprenticeship in Medieval Cities
academic_passage.text: In many medieval European cities, apprenticeship was both an educational arrangement and a social contract. Young people lived with master craftspeople, learned technical skills, and gradually absorbed the customs of a trade. Contracts often specified food, lodging, years of service, and limits on wages. Although apprenticeships could provide opportunities for advancement, they also reinforced hierarchy because masters controlled access to tools, clients, and professional recognition. Surviving contracts therefore reveal not only how skills were taught but also how urban economies organized labor.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The educational and social role of apprenticeship

questions.q: What did apprentices receive according to the passage?
options: Training and often food and lodging

questions.q: Why did apprenticeships reinforce hierarchy?
options: Masters controlled access to important resources.

questions.q: The word “specified” is closest in meaning to
What can surviving contracts reveal?
options: How labor and training were organized

questions.q: What can be inferred about master craftspeople?
options: They had significant authority over apprentices.
They were not involved in training.

academic_talks.title: Mangrove Forests
academic_talks.text: Today we will look at mangrove forests, which grow along tropical and subtropical coastlines. Mangroves tolerate salty water partly by filtering salt at their roots and partly by storing or excreting excess salt through their leaves. Their tangled root systems slow waves and trap sediment, creating sheltered areas where young fish can develop. For coastal communities, mangroves can reduce storm damage, but they are often removed for construction or aquaculture. Restoration projects are most successful when they consider water flow, soil conditions, and local use of the shoreline rather than simply planting seedlings in any available muddy area.

academic_talks.title: Working Memory
academic_talks.text: In cognitive psychology, working memory refers to the limited system we use to hold and manipulate information for a short time. It is involved when you calculate a tip in your head, follow complex directions, or compare two ideas while reading. Researchers often distinguish working memory from long-term memory because its capacity is much smaller and its contents change quickly. However, the two systems interact. For example, background knowledge can reduce the load on working memory by allowing a person to group separate details into meaningful patterns. This is one reason experts can solve familiar problems more efficiently than beginners.

options: By grouping details into meaningful patterns

academic_talks.title: Glacial Landscapes
academic_talks.text: In today’s lecture, we are considering how glaciers shape landscapes. As a glacier moves, it can scrape rock from the valley floor and carry loose material within the ice. This process often leaves valleys with steep sides and broad, flat bottoms. When a glacier melts, it may deposit a mixture of clay, sand, gravel, and boulders known as till. Streams from melting ice can also sort sediment by size, creating layered deposits some distance from the glacier. By examining these features, geologists can reconstruct the direction of ice movement and estimate how far glaciers once extended.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How glaciers shape and leave evidence in landscapes
Why all valleys are formed by rivers
How clay is used in construction
Why modern glaciers no longer move

questions.q: What can a moving glacier do?
options: Scrape rock and carry loose material
Sort every sediment inside the ice

questions.q: What is till?
options: A mixed deposit left by melting ice

questions.q: How can meltwater streams affect sediment?
options: They can sort it by size.
They turn it into solid ice.
They remove all boulders from valleys.

questions.q: What can geologists infer from glacial features?
options: The direction and extent of past ice movement
The exact temperature of every winter
The age of all nearby trees
The chemical formula of every rock

academic_talks.title: Language Borrowing
academic_talks.text: Languages frequently borrow words when speakers come into contact through trade, migration, conquest, or popular culture. Borrowed words often enter a language along with new objects or ideas, but they may change in pronunciation or meaning after adoption. For example, a word associated with a specific food in one language may become a general restaurant term in another. Linguists study borrowing because it reveals historical contact between communities and shows that languages are not closed systems. Even languages with strong literary traditions continue to adapt when speakers need new ways to describe experience.

questions.q: What is the main topic of the talk?
options: Why and how languages borrow words

questions.q: What can cause borrowing?
options: Contact through trade, migration, conquest, or culture
A refusal to name new objects

questions.q: What may happen to borrowed words?
options: Their pronunciation or meaning may change.
They always keep exactly the same meaning.

questions.q: Why do linguists study borrowing?
options: It reveals historical contact between communities.
It proves languages are closed systems.

questions.q: What does the talk imply about languages with literary traditions?
options: They can still change over time.
